notes: Migrated from the original Chroma store and training data, plus general wellness reference notes. Used for optional retrieval only.

documents.title: Migrated memory 1
documents.text: You are strong and capable! Every day is a new chance.

documents.title: Migrated memory 2
documents.text: Don't give up now. Great things take time!

documents.title: Migrated memory 3
documents.text: Even small steps move you forward.

documents.title: I feel overwhelmed with studies and deadlines.
documents.text: It's completely okay to feel overwhelmed sometimes. Let’s take a deep breath and break it down step by step. You're not alone in this.

documents.title: I'm happy today! I got great marks.
documents.text: That’s fantastic! I'm really proud of you. Your hard work is paying off—keep shining!

documents.title: I failed my exam again. I feel useless.
documents.text: I'm really sorry you're feeling this way. Failing an exam doesn't define your worth. You have value beyond results. Let’s talk about how to move forward.

documents.title: Can you motivate me for tomorrow's test?
documents.text: Of course! You’ve prepared for this, and you’ve got the strength to do well. Believe in yourself. One step at a time—you’re doing great!

documents.title: I had a perfect day today. Everything went smoothly.
documents.text: That’s so lovely to hear! Savor those moments—they’re special and you deserve them!

documents.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
documents.text: A grounding exercise for anxious moments: notice 5 things you can see, 4 you can physically feel, 3 you can hear, 2 you can smell, and 1 you can taste. Go slowly, and name each one. The aim is to bring attention back to the present, not to make anxiety disappear instantly.

documents.title: A longer exhale
documents.text: When stress is high, try a longer exhale: breathe in through the nose for about 4 counts, then out for about 6. Repeat 5–10 times. A longer exhale can gently activate the body’s calming response. If breathing deeply feels uncomfortable, return to your natural breath.

documents.title: Study stress
documents.text: For study stress, choose one small task that can be finished in 15–25 minutes. Put the phone out of reach, set a timer, and take a real break afterwards. Progress on one small piece is more useful than planning the perfect revision day. Sleep and food are part of preparation, not distractions from it.

documents.title: When everything feels heavy
documents.text: On a low day, lower the bar rather than pushing harder: one glass of water, one window opened, one message to someone safe. If low mood lasts most days for weeks, or makes daily life hard, talking to a doctor or mental-health professional is a practical next step, not a failure.

documents.title: Loneliness
documents.text: Loneliness can make reaching out feel risky. Start with a low-pressure message to one person — “I’ve been thinking of you, how are you?” — rather than waiting until you have something impressive to say. Connection is a skill we practise, not a test we pass.

documents.title: Self-compassion
documents.text: Self-compassion is not letting yourself off the hook; it is treating yourself as someone you care about. Try naming what happened without insults (“I missed the deadline and I feel ashamed”), then ask what you would say to a friend in the same situation. You can take responsibility and still be kind to yourself.

documents.title: Sleep and worry
documents.text: If worry keeps you awake, write the unfinished thought or task on paper with one next step for tomorrow. Keep the room dim and avoid checking the clock. If sleep problems persist for weeks, mention them to a healthcare professional, especially if they affect safety or daily functioning.

documents.title: Boundaries
documents.text: A boundary can be short and kind: “I can’t take that on this week, but I can help with one part next Tuesday.” You do not need a long justification. Boundaries protect the energy you need for the things you care about.

documents.title: Anger
documents.text: Anger often points to a boundary or unmet need. Before responding, give yourself a pause: unclench your jaw, feel your feet, and name the need underneath (“I need to be heard”). Wait until the first surge passes if you can. If anger is frightening you or others, seek professional support.

documents.title: Asking for help
documents.text: You do not have to be in crisis to deserve support. If something has felt heavy for more than a couple of weeks, a GP, counsellor, therapist, faith leader, or trusted friend can be a first point of contact. Ask what is available, and it is okay to say “I’m not sure what I need yet.”

documents.title: Savouring good moments
documents.text: When something good happens, pause for ten seconds and notice the details: what you can see, who is there, how your body feels. Savouring helps a good moment land. You can also write down one specific thing that went well and why it mattered.

documents.title: Procrastination
documents.text: Procrastination is often a reaction to feeling overwhelmed or afraid of doing it badly, not laziness. Shrink the first step until it feels almost too easy — open the document, write one sentence, set a five-minute timer. You can stop after five minutes; often you will not need to.
